# Clipboard Health Staffing Project: Metric Glossary

These are the definitions used by the staffing pipeline (`clipboard_health_pipeline`, dbt project `clipboard_health`), the staffing dashboard, and this assistant. Where a project definition differs from CMS's own calculation, the difference is stated.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## HPRD (hours per resident day)
HPRD is total direct-care nurse hours divided by total resident-days. It is always a weighted measure: hours and resident-days are summed first, then divided. A simple average of daily or facility HPRDs is never used, because it gives a 30-bed facility the same weight as a 300-bed facility.

- Facility-quarter HPRD = sum of nurse hours across the quarter / sum of daily MDS census across the quarter (`MART_FACILITY_QUARTER.HPRD`).
- State-quarter HPRD = sum of nurse hours for all facilities in the state / sum of their resident-days (`MART_STATE_QUARTER.HPRD`).
- National HPRD = the same calculation across all facilities.

Resident-days come from the daily MDS census (`MDSCENSUS` in the PBJ file). Days with zero census are dropped before any calculation, as in the original Data Analyst project.

source: Project metric glossary
location: section: Nurse hours used in this project
text:
## Nurse hours used in this project
Nurse hours = RN hours + LPN hours + CNA hours (`HRS_RN + HRS_LPN + HRS_CNA`), each including both employee and contract hours.

This is narrower than CMS's "total nurse staffing" in the PBJ public use file exclusion rules, which also counts RN Director of Nursing, RN and LPN with administrative duties, Medication Aide/Technician, and Nurse Aide in Training hours. Director of Nursing and administrative hours are loaded but are not part of project HPRD. Because of this, project HPRD is slightly lower than a figure computed with every CMS nursing category.

Data cleaning: Director of Nursing hours are capped at 24 per day, because the Data Analyst project found entries above 24 hours in a single day.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Contract share
Contract share = contract nurse hours / total nurse hours, where contract nurse hours = RN contract + LPN contract + CNA contract hours (`HRS_RN_CTR + HRS_LPN_CTR + HRS_CNA_CTR`). In PBJ, "contract" covers agency and contract staff who are not on the facility's payroll; CMS requires facilities to report their hours along with employee hours.

A facility with zero nurse hours gets a contract share of 0. State and national contract shares are weighted the same way as HPRD: sum contract hours, sum nurse hours, then divide.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Reporting gap (IS_REPORTING_GAP)
A facility-quarter is flagged as a reporting gap when its quarter HPRD is below 0.5 (dbt variable `reporting_gap_hprd`). Real nursing homes do not staff at under half an hour of nursing care per resident per day, so these records almost certainly have missing payroll submissions rather than real staffing levels.

Reporting-gap facilities are excluded from all national, state, and percentage figures by default. This matches the published dashboard, `MART_STATE_QUARTER` (which already excludes them), and the pipeline's regression test. About 20 facilities were flagged in Q2 2024 and 14 in Q2 2026. Including them lowers national HPRD slightly (for example 3.29 instead of 3.30 for Q2 2024).

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Below 3.0 HPRD (BELOW_REFERENCE)
`BELOW_REFERENCE` is TRUE when a facility's quarter HPRD is under 3.0 (dbt variable `hprd_reference`). The 3.0 line is an analysis reference carried over from the Data Analyst project. It is not a federal or state regulatory requirement. The percentage of facilities below 3.0 is the share of non-reporting-gap facilities with `BELOW_REFERENCE` TRUE.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Low-staffing day
A low-staffing day is a facility-day with daily HPRD under 1.5 (dbt variable `low_day_hprd`), counted in `FCT_FACILITY_DAY.IS_LOW_DAY`. `MART_FACILITY_QUARTER.DAYS_BELOW_LOW_THRESHOLD` counts them per facility per quarter.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Watchlist facility
A watchlist facility has 10 or more low-staffing days in a quarter (`DAYS_BELOW_LOW_THRESHOLD >= 10`). `MART_STATE_QUARTER.WATCHLIST_FACILITIES` counts them by state, excluding reporting-gap facilities.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Quarter-over-quarter change
`MART_FACILITY_QUARTER.HPRD_CHANGE` and `CONTRACT_SHARE_CHANGE` compare a facility's quarter with its previous loaded quarter (`PREV_QUARTER`). The loaded quarters are 2024Q2, 2025Q3, 2025Q4, 2026Q1 and 2026Q2, so the change into 2025Q3 is measured against 2024Q2, which is five quarters apart, not one.

source: Project metric glossary

## Quarters loaded and data sources
Quarters are written like `2024Q2`. The pipeline loads PBJ Daily Nurse Staffing for 2024Q2 (to reconcile with the Data Analyst project) and 2025Q3 through 2026Q2, plus the latest monthly CMS Provider Information snapshot (star ratings, ownership, certified beds, location). Questions about other quarters cannot be answered from this data.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Data quality checks
- Row counts: the rows loaded into Snowflake must equal the rows in each source file. This test exists because an Excel export in the first version of the project silently cut the data off at 1,048,575 rows.
- Daily plausibility: a warning-level test flags facility-days with negative hours or more than 24 nursing hours per resident (247 facility-days across 5 quarters, fewer than 1 in 25,000). They are kept but reviewed rather than silently dropped.
- Regression: Q2 2024 must reproduce the published dashboard: national HPRD 3.30, 34% of facilities below 3.0, and 7.7% contract share.

source: Project metric glossary
text:
## Tables (Snowflake CLIPBOARD_HEALTH.MARTS)
- `FCT_FACILITY_DAY`: one row per facility per day with residents present.
- `DIM_FACILITY`: one row per facility: name, city, state, ownership type, certified beds, overall and staffing star ratings.
- `MART_FACILITY_QUARTER`: one row per facility per quarter: weighted HPRD, contract share, reporting-gap and below-3.0 flags, low-staffing days, quarter-over-quarter change, facility attributes.
- `MART_STATE_QUARTER`: one row per state per quarter (reporting gaps excluded): HPRD, share below 3.0, contract share, share with no contract staff, watchlist count.
- `MART_STATE_DAY`: one row per state per day, for trend lines.

2. Aggregation 
The staffing data in the PBJ PUFs are aggregated to the facility-day. This means that all included facilities 
will have one record (or row of data) for each day in the quarter. This will range from 90-92 records 
depending on the number of days in the quarter but for a given quarter will be the same for all included 
facilities. Thus, the total number of records in the file will be equal to the number of included facilities 
multiplied by the number of calendar days in the quarter.

a. Facility Inclusion Criteria 
In order to be included in the PBJ PUF, nursing homes must have been active on last day of the 
quarterly submission period. If a facility meets in the inclusion criteria for the nursing PUF for a given 
quarter, that facility will also be included in the non-nursing PUF for the same quarter.

5. MDS-Based Resident Census 
The method used to calculate the daily resident census using MDS data is as follows: 
1) Identify the reporting period (quarter) for which the census will be calculated (e.g., CY 2021 Q1: 
January 1 – March 31, 2021). 
2) Extract MDS assessment data for all residents of a facility beginning one year prior to the 
reporting period to identify all residents that may reside in the facility (i.e., any resident with an 
MDS assessment may still reside in the facility). For example, for the CY 2021 Q1 reporting 
period, extract MDS data from January 1, 2020 through March 31, 2021. 
3) Identify discharged residents using the following criteria: 
a) If a resident has a MDS discharge assessment, use the discharge date reported on that 
assessment and assume that the resident no longer resides in the facility as of the date of 
discharge on the last assessment. If there is a subsequent admission assessment, then 
assume that the resident re-entered the nursing home on the entry date indicated on the 
admission assessment. 
b) For any resident with an interval o

6. Data Limitations and Caveats 
These Public Use Files are being made available to facilitate analysis and exploration of this richly 
detailed source of staffing information about US Nursing Homes. However, there are some limitations 
that are worth noting: 
• There may be some instances where data submitted by a facility may not be a full 
representation of the hours staff actually worked. There may be some erroneous reporting as 
some providers continue to fine-tune their data submissions.

• The staffing measures previously displayed on the Nursing Home Compare website were derived 
from data reported on the CMS-671 and 672 forms. We do not expect data from these forms to 
exactly match the PBJ data for several reasons. (Note: Staffing data is no longer being collected 
on the CMS-671 form as of June 1, 2018).

CHAPTER 1: Overview 
1.1 Introduction

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) has long identified staffing as 
one of the vital components of a nursing home’s ability to provide quality care. Over 
time, CMS has utilized staffing data for a myriad of purposes in an effort to more 
accurately and effectively gauge its impact on quality of care in nursing homes. Staffing 
information is also posted on the CMS Nursing Home Compare website, and it is used in 
the Nursing Home Five Star Quality Rating System to help consumers understand the 
level and differences of staffing in nursing homes.

Section 6106 of the Affordable Care Act requires facilities to electronically submit direct 
care staffing information (including agency and contract staff) based on payroll and 
other auditable data. The data, when combined with census information, can then be 
used to not only report on the level of staff in each nursing home, but also to report on 
employee turnover and tenure, which can impact the quality of care delivered.

2.4 Census

CMS uses Minimum Data Set (MDS) data to calculate a daily resident census for each 
facility. The method that CMS uses to calculate the daily resident census using MDS data is 
as follows: 
1) Identify the reporting period (quarter) for which the census will be calculated (e.g., 
Q1 FY 2017: October 1, 2016 – December 31, 2016).

2) Extract MDS assessment data for all residents of a facility beginning one year prior to the 
reporting period to identify all residents that may reside in the facility (i.e., any resident 
with an MDS assessment may still reside in the facility). For example, using the example 
reporting period in #1 above, CMS would extract MDS data from October 1, 2015 
through December 31, 2016.

with an MDS assessment may still reside in the facility). For example, using the example 
reporting period in #1 above, CMS would extract MDS data from October 1, 2015 
through December 31, 2016.

3) Identify discharged residents using the following criteria: 
a. If a resident has a MDS discharge assessment, use the discharge date reported on 
that assessment and assume that the resident no longer resides in the facility as 
of that date. If there is a subsequent admission assessment, then assume that 
the resident re-entered the nursing home on the entry date indicated on the 
admission assessment. 
b. For any resident with an interval of 150 days or more with no assessment, 
assume the resident no longer resides in the facility as of the 150th day from the 
last assessment. (This assumption is based on the requirement for facilities to 
complete MDS assessments on all residents at least quarterly. If no assessment is 
present, assume the resident was discharged, but the facility did not transmit a 
discharge assessment).

Section II – Skilled Nursing Facility Quality Reporting Program (SNF QRP) 
Introduction to the SNF QRP Program 
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Care Compare website provides a single user-friendly 
interface that consumers can use to understand information about nursing homes, doctors, long-term care 
hospitals, and other health care services instead of searching through multiple tools. Care Compare enables 
patients and caregivers to make informed decisions about healthcare based on cost, quality of care, volume 
of services, and other data. Information about the quality measures on Care Compare are presented similarly 
and clearly across all provider types and care settings. Consumers can select multiple facilities and compare 
their performance on various quality metrics. To access the Care Compare website, please visit 
https://www.medicare.gov/care-compare.
